title: Degreasing vs General-Purpose Cleaning
excerpt: General-purpose cleaning handles mixed routine soil; degreasing is a targeted process for oily or fatty deposits and may require different chemistry, dwell, temperature, mechanical action and recovery.
content_html:
General-purpose cleaning and degreasing overlap, but they are not identical. General-purpose cleaning is designed for everyday mixed soil across compatible surfaces. Degreasing focuses specifically on oily, fatty or grease-rich contamination that resists lighter cleaning.

The soil determines the process

The 2026 FDA Food Code states that wet-cleaning procedures should be selected according to the equipment or utensil and the type of soil to be removed. This is the core difference: a light dust-and-food film does not necessarily require the same chemistry as fryer grease.

General-purpose cleaning

General-purpose cleaners are useful for routine soil such as light food film, dust, fingerprints and mixed environmental soil where heavy grease is not dominant.

Degreasing

Degreasing may use stronger wetting, emulsifying or alkaline chemistry, higher compatible temperature, longer dwell and more mechanical action to detach grease. The method still has to remain compatible with the surface.

Comparison

FeatureGeneral-purpose cleaningDegreasing
Main soilLight mixed routine soilFats, oils and heavy grease
ChemistryBroad light-duty cleanerGrease-targeted chemistry
Dwell/actionUsually lowerMay need more dwell/action
RecoveryRemove routine soil/residueCritical to prevent grease redeposition
Typical triggerRoutine schedule/visible soilGrease-rich deposit or film

Why general-purpose cleaner may fail on heavy grease

A light-duty product may wet the surface without fully emulsifying a thick grease layer. Repeated wiping can then spread the deposit into a thinner but still greasy film.

Why degreaser is not always the better choice

Stronger chemistry can increase material risk, residue burden and worker exposure. If routine soil can be removed with a milder compatible cleaner, a heavy-duty degreaser adds no automatic benefit.

Food-contact surfaces still need the full hygiene process

When degreasing food-contact surfaces, follow the applicable requirements for rinsing and sanitizing after cleaning before the surface returns to use.

Practical takeaway

Choose the process from the soil, not the product label. Use general-purpose cleaning for light mixed soil and targeted degreasing when fats and oils are the dominant problem.

References

  1. U.S. FDA — FDA Food Code 2026, Chapter 4.
  2. U.S. FDA — Food Code 2026.
